claim_verdicts.evidence: Could not re-run: the loop version was never committed (repo clean at 4fca60a, `git status` empty), so I treat the author's recorded live run as the evidence. Corroborated what I could: `select customer_id, count(*) from orders group by customer_id` on donhang-db returns customer_id 1 -> 7, so 1 + 7 = 8 is arithmetically the N+1 count. Per-iteration LINQ queries do round-trip each time (EF Core docs: "another query *per blog*... this is sometimes called the *N+1* problem").
claim_verdicts.source: live: docker exec donhang-db psql -c 'select customer_id, count(*) from orders group by customer_id'; efcore-docs entity-framework/core/performance/efficient-querying.md

claim_verdicts.evidence: Re-ran live on the stage-1 lab: set log_statement='all', logged in as anh.tran@example.com, called GET /api/v1/orders (HTTP 200, 7 entries). donhang-db logged exactly one statement for the call: "execute <unnamed>: SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.placed_at, o.status, c.id, c.city, c.email, c.full_name, c.password_hash FROM orders AS o INNER JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.customer_id = $1 ORDER BY o.id". log_statement reset to 'none' afterwards (verified via SHOW).
claim_verdicts.source: live run 2026-09-24 on donhang-db / donhang-api (stage-1 lab)

claim_verdicts.evidence: efficient-querying.md, "Beware of lazy loading": "each iteration in the inner foreach triggers an additional database query, in its own roundtrip. As a result, after the initial query loading all the blogs, we then have another query *per blog*, loading all its posts; this is sometimes called the *N+1* problem"; and "Because lazy loading makes it extremely easy to inadvertently trigger the N+1 problem, it is recommended to avoid it. Eager or explicit loading make it very clear in the source code when a database roundtrip occurs."

`git show stage-1:DonHang.Infrastructure/EfOrderRepository.cs` lines 9-14 are character-for-character what the lesson quotes: FindAsync = `db.Orders.Include(o => o.Items).FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id)`; ListByCustomerAsync = `db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId).Include(o => o.Customer).OrderBy(o => o.Id).ToListAsync()`. One Include each.

`git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Controllers/OrdersController.cs` lines 48-56 match the quoted block exactly, including `[Authorize]`, `[HttpGet]`, `int.Parse(User.FindFirstValue(JwtRegisteredClaimNames.Sub)!)` and `orders.Select(o => new OrderSummaryDto(o.Id, o.Status, o.Customer!.FullName)).ToList()`. Class-level `[Route("api/v1/orders")]` (line 11) confirms the route the lesson names.

No lazy loading is configured: `git grep` over stage-1 finds no UseLazyLoadingProxies / Proxies package; the only registration is `services.AddDbContext<DonHangDbContext>(options => options.UseNpgsql(connectionString))`. But "or left null" is too absolute: eager.md tip: "Entity Framework Core will automatically fix-up navigation properties to any other entities that were previously loaded into the context instance. So even if you don't explicitly include the data for a navigation property, the property may still be populated..."
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: DonHangDbContext configures no lazy loading, so accessing order.Customer never triggers a query; it is populated only if the query eager-loaded it with Include, or if that customer was already loaded into the same DbContext instance (navigation fix-up). Otherwise it stays null.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Orphaned claim added after this round's own review ran, to close the major issue on single-query mode being an unlisted assumption (see issues[3], section 5). Verified using the same source already cited in that issue's fix: entity-framework/core/querying/single-split-queries.md states EF Core folds related entities into the primary query via JOINs ("EF loads related entities by introducing JOINs into a single query") and that "EF Core uses single query mode by default in the absence of any configuration", with AsSplitQuery/UseQuerySplittingBehavior as the only overrides.

issues.text: Arithmetic contradicts the lesson's own N+1 formula and section 4. With two orders the loop version sends 1 + 2 = 3 calls, not 2. Section 4 already says "for a customer with one order, the loop version costs two calls against `.Include`'s one", and quiz q6's option-d explanation says "2 to 4 total for 1-3 orders" — both incompatible with the sentence as written.
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "the extra cost starts at the second row: three calls instead of one for a customer with just two orders." (Or keep "two calls instead of one" and change the example to a customer with one order.)
issues.quote: the extra cost starts at the second row: two calls instead of one for a customer with just two orders

issues.text: The marked key (a, ~61) and the rejection of option b both assume `db.Products.FindAsync(id)` always queries. EF Core docs: "Find first checks if the entity is already tracked, and if so returns the entity immediately. A database query is only made if the entity is not tracked locally." With 60 item reads over a repeating product catalogue, the real count is 1 + (number of distinct products), so ~61 only holds if all 60 products differ. Distractor b's explanation ("a product ordered many times gets queried many times") is flatly wrong.
issues.fix: Change the call in the stem to one that always round-trips, e.g. `await db.Products.FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Id == item.ProductId)`, and keep key (a); rewrite b's explanation to "nothing here groups the item reads into one query per distinct product". If `FindAsync` must stay, the key has to become "1 + one per distinct product" and the lesson must first teach change-tracker lookups.
issues.quote: Around 61 — 1 for the orders, plus roughly one more per item across every order

issues.text: The question asks to order four facts "in the order they happen", but option c describes the shipped `.Include` version, which is a separate execution with its own timeline — it does not happen after b and before d in any observable sense. c could equally be placed first. The key a-b-c-d is therefore arbitrary, not derivable from the lesson.
issues.fix: Either drop c and d's cross-version framing (order only the loop version's three steps, then its total), or restate the stem as "the order the lesson presents them" and make c explicitly the after-the-fact comparison, e.g. "Re-running the same request on the shipped version returns the same 3 orders in one query".
issues.quote: Put these four facts about a customer with 3 orders in the order they happen

issues.text: Wrong entity: the query in this lesson returns a customer's orders (`db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId).Include(o => o.Customer)`), so the list whose size varies is the order list; the customer list has exactly one row here. As written a junior reads it as if `.Include` were loading a list of customers.
issues.fix: Replace with: "Whether the order list has one row or a thousand, that query count stays exactly one".
issues.quote: Whether the customer list has one row or a thousand, that query count stays exactly one

issues.text: Unlisted claim: "one `.Include(...)` call, one JOIN, one query, regardless of how many `OrderItem` rows an order has" (and the same assertion in sections 3 and 4). This is true only because EF Core's default is single-query mode for collection navigations — configurable per query (`AsSplitQuery`) or globally (`UseQuerySplittingBehavior`). It is version/configuration dependent and is not in the claims ledger.
issues.fix: Add a claim with version_key efcore citing entity-framework/core/querying/single-split-queries.md ("EF loads related entities by introducing JOINs into a single query"; "EF Core uses single query mode by default in the absence of any configuration"), and add the condition to the prose: "with EF Core's default single-query behaviour, which this project does not change".
issues.quote: one `.Include(...)` call, one JOIN, one query, regardless of how many `OrderItem` rows an order has

issues.text: "query each order's customer separately" does not say how. All 7 orders belong to the same customer, so a loop written with `db.Customers.FindAsync(o.CustomerId)` would send 2 statements, not 8 (Find returns a tracked entity without querying). The 8 in the situation and in claim 1 holds only for a LINQ query per iteration.
issues.fix: Name the shape: "...loop over them and run a query for each order's customer (`db.Customers.FirstOrDefaultAsync(c => c.Id == o.CustomerId)`)". Same wording in the ledger's claim 1 text.
issues.quote: loop over them and query each order's customer separately

issues.text: "would leave `order.Customer` `null`" ignores EF Core navigation fix-up: a customer already loaded into the same DbContext instance is attached to the navigation without any Include. True for this request path (List() loads nothing else), but stated as a general rule.
issues.fix: Add the condition: "...would leave `order.Customer` `null` unless that customer had already been loaded into the same DbContext instance." Update claim 6 accordingly.
issues.quote: would leave `order.Customer` `null`, not slow

issues.text: `.Include(...)` is not a LINQ call: it is an EF Core extension method on `IQueryable<T>` (EF Core docs: "You can use the `Include` method to specify related data to be included in query results"). Calling it "the LINQ call" muddles the boundary the prereq lesson draws between LINQ and EF Core.
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "`.Include(...)` — the EF Core method you chain onto a LINQ query to ask for eager loading".
issues.quote: `.Include(...)` — the LINQ call that asks EF Core for eager loading

issues.text: Unlisted comparative claim with no source and no condition. Whether the joined query costs the server more than one plain SELECT depends on indexes, row width and duplication; the docs discuss the risk only as cartesian explosion for collection navigations, not as a general rule.
issues.fix: Either drop the clause, or condition it: "the joined query returns wider rows (the customer's columns repeat on every order row), but PostgreSQL still only gets asked once".
issues.quote: the database does more work per query, but PostgreSQL still only gets asked once

issues.text: The Try it steps cannot produce the stated expected result. Counting response entries shows nothing about query counts; the learner never sees a query log, so "still runs exactly one query" is asserted, not observed. I confirmed the one-query fact myself only by turning on `log_statement='all'` on donhang-db, which the steps never mention.
issues.fix: Either add a step that shows the statement (e.g. `docker exec donhang-db psql -U donhang -d donhang -c "ALTER SYSTEM SET log_statement='all'" -c 'select pg_reload_conf()'`, repeat the call, `docker logs donhang-db`, then reset), or restate the expected result as something the current steps do show (every entry carries `customerName`, filled by the one query's JOIN).
issues.quote: however many orders come back, `ListByCustomerAsync` still runs exactly one query to produce them all

beyond_scope: quiz q5 requires knowing that `DbSet.FindAsync` serves already-tracked entities from the change tracker without querying — a behaviour the lesson never teaches (see the q5 blocker)

issues.text: Before you start tells me I already know "a query built with LINQ", but the only prerequisite listed is saving-changes, whose five lines are about AddAsync, SaveChangesAsync, one transaction and generated ids - nothing about LINQ or about when a query runs. LINQ then carries the Core concepts bullet for `.Include` ("chain onto a LINQ query"), so the one word that places `.Include` is a word I was never taught. Connections even says querying-with-linq holds "the mechanism this lesson relies on", yet nothing told me to read it first.
issues.quote: you know a change tracker keeps entities in memory, and that a query built with LINQ only reaches PostgreSQL once something asks it for results.
issues.fix: Split the Before you start bullet in two and add the lesson that taught LINQ: "[[backend.l1.querying-with-linq]] - you know a LINQ query is how `EfOrderRepository` asks PostgreSQL for rows, and that it only runs when something asks it for results.", leaving the change tracker half on the saving-changes bullet.

issues.text: The correction to the first misconception turns on "lazy loading", which the lesson never defines and which is not a term I know. I cannot tell whether it is something I would have to switch off, something EF Core does somewhere else, or something that would have made the loop version fine after all. Quiz q2's answer depends on the same undefined term.
issues.quote: this codebase has no lazy loading configured, so a different method that returned orders without `.Include(o => o.Customer)` would leave `order.Customer` `null`
issues.fix: Replace "this codebase has no lazy loading configured, so" with "nothing in this project fills `order.Customer` in by itself when you read it, so" - same point, no new term.

issues.text: "the same `DbContext` instance" is a second unknown in that same sentence. saving-changes taught me a change tracker that keeps entities in memory, but not a class called `DbContext`, and not how far one "instance" of it reaches - one request? one method? one run of the app? Without that I cannot judge the escape clause, which is exactly the part that decides whether `order.Customer` is null.
issues.quote: would leave `order.Customer` `null` unless that customer had already been loaded into the same `DbContext` instance, not slow.
issues.fix: Replace "into the same `DbContext` instance" with "by an earlier query in the same request, into the change tracker" - change tracker is a term saving-changes already gave me.
